aquí.notes: Aquí points to the immediate spot right beside the speaker (aquí tiene = here you go).

arco.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin arcus ('hunting bow, curved vault, rainbow').

arco.notes: Names both an architectural stone arch over a courtyard gallery and a stringed-instrument bow.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: armario

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aromático
Wiktionary — aromático

arquitecto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin architectus ('master builder'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn), a compound of ἀρχι- (arkhi-, 'chief') and τέκτων (téktōn, 'builder, carpenter').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arquitecto
Wiktionary — arquitecto

arreglar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + regla ('rule, straightedge, order') + -ar, ultimately from Latin rēgula ('straight stick, rule, pattern').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arreglar
Wiktionary — arreglar

arriba.etymology: Univerbation of Old Spanish a riba ('up toward the high bank or slope'), from the Latin prepositional phrase ad rīpam ('to the riverbank or steep shore').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: arriba
Wiktionary — arriba

asa.etymology: Inherited from Latin ansa ('handle of a vessel, loop, grip'), showing the regular Vulgar Latin reduction of the cluster -ns- to -s-.

asegurar.etymology: Formed from a- + seguro ('safe, sure, firm') + -ar (or Late Latin assēcūrāre), from Classical Latin sēcūrus ('free from care, safe', from sē- + cūra 'care').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asegurar
Wiktionary — asegurar

asentir.etymology: Borrowed or inherited from Latin assentīre (Classical deponent assentīrī, 'to agree with, approve, give assent'), a compound of ad- + sentīre ('to feel, perceive, judge').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asentir
Wiktionary — asentir

asiento.etymology: Deverbal noun from asentar ('to seat, set down, settle'), descending from Vulgar Latin *assedentāre, built on the present participle stem sedēns, sedentis of Latin sedēre ('to sit').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asiento
Wiktionary — asiento

asomar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + Old Spanish somo ('summit, top, ridge') + -ar, originally meaning 'to come into view over the top of a hill', from Latin summum ('highest point').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asomar
Wiktionary — asomar

asombrado.etymology: Participial adjective of asombrar ('astonished, amazed'), formed from a- + sombra ('shadow, shade', < Vulgar Latin *subumbrāre / umbra), having shifted from 'frightened by a shadow' to 'amazed'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: asombrado
Wiktionary — asombrado

así.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish assí, formed by compounding the preposition a (< Latin ad) with sí (< Latin sīc 'thus, in this way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: así

atado.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from atar ('tied, bound; bundle'), inherited from Latin aptāre ('to fit together, join, fasten').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atado
Wiktionary — atado

atascado.etymology: Participial adjective of atascar ('stuck, clogged, jammed'), formed from a- + tasco ('bundle of coarse flax tow used to plug gaps') + -ar, of pre-Roman (likely Celtic) origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atascado
Wiktionary — atascado

atascar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- + tasco ('bundle of coarse flax tow used for plugging or caulking') + -ar, of pre-Roman (likely Celtic) origin, meaning 'to plug up, obstruct, jam'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atascar
Wiktionary — atascar

atender.etymology: Inherited from Latin attendere ('to stretch toward, direct the mind to, pay attention, wait upon'), formed from ad- + tendere ('to stretch').

history.meaning: to direct one's attention to, heed

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atender
Wiktionary — atender

atornillar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Spanish from a- + tornillo ('screw', diminutive of torno 'lathe, turn', from Latin tornus < Greek τόρνος) + -ar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atornillar
Wiktionary — atornillar

atril.etymology: The DLE derives atril from Old Spanish letril, which came from Late Latin lectorīle ('reading stand', built on lector, 'reader'). Speakers reanalysed initial l- as part of the article, turning el letril into el atril.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atril

atril.notes: Used both for a standing lectern and for the hinged wooden music rest on a piano.

atrás.etymology: Formed by compounding the directional preposition a (< Latin ad) with tras ('behind, after', < Latin trans 'across, beyond').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: atrás
Wiktionary — atrás

aun.etymology: Unstressed proclitic form of aún ('even, including'), inherited from Latin adhūc ('until now, still, even so'), with Romance nasalization of the final syllable.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aviso
Wiktionary — aviso

ay.etymology: Natural expressive interjection of pain, lament, startle, or sighing, corresponding to Latin ai and Ancient Greek αἰ (ai).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ay
Wiktionary — ay

ayer.etymology: Evolved from Old Spanish er prefixed with a-, from Vulgar Latin *ad herī, built on Classical Latin herī ('yesterday').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayer
Wiktionary — ayer

ayudar.etymology: Ayudar continues Latin adiūtāre ('to help, assist'), the frequentative verb built on adiuvāre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayudar

ayudar.notes: Before an infinitive, ayudar links with preposition a (ayudar a llevar la maleta).

ayuntamiento.etymology: Derived from ayuntar ('to join, gather, assemble') + -miento, where ayuntar descends from Late Latin adiunctāre, frequentative of Classical Latin adiungere ('to join to, unite').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ayuntamiento
Wiktionary — ayuntamiento

azul.etymology: Azul entered Spanish through Hispanic Arabic lazawárd, from Arabic lāzaward and Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'), with rebracketing of initial l- as part of the article.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azul

azul.notes: Plural is azules; when modified by a shade word like azul oscuro ('dark blue'), the compound shade phrase stays invariable.

azúcar.etymology: Azúcar comes from Hispanic Arabic assúkkar, continuing Classical Arabic sukkar, Persian šakar, and ultimately Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, candied sugar crystals').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: azúcar

azúcar.notes: Commonly masculine in everyday Spain (el azúcar blanco/moreno), though the DLE accepts both masculine and feminine agreement.

año.etymology: Año descends from Latin annus. The Latin double n and the Spanish ñ give a useful visible connection between the older and modern forms of the word for a year.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: año

año.notes: Keep ñ in both año and años. The word names a period of twelve months and also occurs in the Spanish way of giving someone’s age.

aún.etymology: Stressed temporal adverb ('still, yet'), inherited from Latin adhūc ('until now, hitherto, still'), with loss of final -c and nasalization in Ibero-Romance.

history.meaning: up to this time, still, yet

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: aún

bajar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre ('to lower, go down'), derived from Late Latin bassus ('low, short in stature').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bajar
Wiktionary — bajar

bajo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus ('thick, short, low'), with the palatal consonant of Old Spanish baxo influenced by the verb baxar (< *bassiāre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bajo
Wiktionary — bajo

balda.etymology: Originally a northern Spanish term for a wall or cupboard shelf, adopted into general Peninsular Spanish; of uncertain origin, linked by the DLE and Corominas to Basque balda ('shelf').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: balda
Wiktionary — balda

bandeja.etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese bandeja ('tray, winnowing fan'), derived from bandejar ('to rock from side to side, sift grain'), built on banda ('side').

history.meaning: to sway from side to side, winnow

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bandeja
Wiktionary — bandeja

banquito.etymology: Formed within Spanish from banco ('bench, stool') + the diminutive suffix -ito; banco was borrowed from Germanic *bankiz ('bench, raised shelf').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: banco

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barrer
Wiktionary — barrer

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: barrio

barrio.notes: Names a distinct town neighbourhood with its own local shops, squares and daily life.

base.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin basis ('pedestal, foundation, base'), from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, 'stepping, foot, base'), derived from βαίνειν (baínein, 'to step, go').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: basura
Wiktionary — basura

batir.etymology: Descends from Vulgar Latin *battĕre, reduced from Classical Latin battuĕre ('to beat, strike, pound').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: batir

batir.notes: In cooking, batir means 'to whisk or beat' eggs, cream, or lemon curd.

baño.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *banneum for Classical Latin balneum ('bath, bathhouse'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon, 'bathing room').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: billete

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bisagra

bizcocho.etymology: Bizcocho continues Latin bis coctus ('twice baked'), originally naming crisp ship's biscuit dried twice in the oven before shifting in Spain to light sponge cake.

Wiktionary — bolsillo

Wiktionary — borde

bordillo.etymology: Diminutive formed in Spanish from borde ('edge, rim', < French bord < Frankish *bord) + -illo, designating the raised stone curb bordering a sidewalk.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bordillo
Wiktionary — bordillo

Wiktionary — bosque

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: bote
Wiktionary — bote

botella.etymology: Borrowed from French bouteille ('bottle'), which evolved from Late Latin butticula ('small flask or cask'), diminutive of buttis ('cask, wineskin').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: botella
Wiktionary — botella

botón.etymology: Borrowed from Old French boton (modern bouton, 'flower bud, knob, button'), derived from boter ('to push out, sprout'), from Frankish *bōtan ('to push, strike').

Wiktionary — botón

a toast / to drink a toast

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: brocha
Wiktionary — brocha

brochazo.etymology: Formed within Spanish from brocha ('paintbrush') + the suffix -azo denoting a stroke or blow ('brushstroke').

bueno.etymology: Bueno continues Latin bonus ('good'), with stressed short Latin ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

bueno.notes: Shortens to buen directly before a masculine singular noun (buen viaje, buen sitio), and gives the plural greeting ¡Buenos días!.

buhardilla.etymology: Diminutive of buharda ('skylight, garret window, attic'), originally a roof vent for smoke, likely related to Old French bouffarde / bouffer ('to puff, blow out smoke').

buscar.notes: Buscar already includes the English 'for' inside the verb: busco mis llaves (never *busco por mis llaves).

Wiktionary — cabezota

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colina

colina.notes: Names a gentle hill smaller than una montaña.

colocar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin collocāre ('to put in place, arrange, station'), formed from com- + locāre (from locus 'place'), a doublet of inherited colgar.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: colocar
Wiktionary — colocar

color.etymology: Inherited from Latin color, colōris ('hue, tint, complexion').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: color

color.notes: Masculine in standard Spanish (el color), whereas several sister Romance nouns became feminine.

columna.etymology: The DLE records columna as a learned borrowing/retention from Latin columna ('pillar, support').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: columna

columna.notes: Used both for architectural stone pillars and for vertical columns of figures in a notebook.

comer.etymology: Inherited from Latin comedere ('to eat up, consume entirely'), an intensive compound of com- + edere ('to eat') that replaced simple edere in Ibero-Romance.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comer
Wiktionary — comer

comercial.etymology: Derived from comercio ('trade, commerce') + -al (reinforced by French commercial), from Latin commercium ('trade, traffic', from com- + merx 'merchandise').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comercial
Wiktionary — comercial

como.etymology: Unaccented como develops from Vulgar Latin *quōmodo (from Classical Latin quō modo, 'in what manner'), functioning in modern Spanish for comparisons ('like, as') and causal clauses ('since').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: como

como.notes: Compare unaccented como ('like, as'; also 'I eat' from comer) with accented ¿cómo? ('how? / pardon?').

compartir.etymology: Inherited or borrowed from Late Latin compartīre (Classical deponent compartīrī, 'to divide with another, share'), from com- + partīre (built on pars, partis 'part').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compartir
Wiktionary — compartir

compañera.etymology: Feminine form of compañero ('companion, partner, colleague'), derived from Old Spanish compaño (< Late Latin compāniō, -ōnis 'one who shares bread').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compañero
Wiktionary — compañera

compañero.etymology: Derived with -ero from Old Spanish compaño, from Late Latin compāniō, compāniōnis ('one who eats bread with another'), formed from com- ('with') + pānis ('bread').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compañero
Wiktionary — compañero

completamente.etymology: Adverb formed within Spanish from the feminine adjective completa ('complete, full', < Latin complētus) + the suffix -mente (< Latin mente 'with a ... mind').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: completamente
Wiktionary — completamente

completo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin complētus ('filled up, full, complete'), past participle of complēre (com- + plēre 'to fill').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: completo
Wiktionary — completo

componer.etymology: Componer continues Latin componĕre ('to put together, arrange'), formed from com- ('together') and ponĕre ('to place').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: componer

componer.notes: Shares all stem irregularities of poner (compongo, compuso, compuesto).

compositora.etymology: Feminine form of compositor, learned borrowing from Latin compositor, compositōris ('one who puts together, arranger, author'), from compōnere ('to put together, compose').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compositor

comprador.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin comparātor, comparātōris ('buyer, purchaser') or derived in Spanish from comprar ('to buy') + the agent suffix -dor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comprador
Wiktionary — comprador

comprar.etymology: Inherited from Latin comparāre ('to get ready, procure, furnish, purchase'), with regular syncope of the unstressed internal vowel.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: comprar
Wiktionary — comprar

compás.etymology: Deverbal noun from compasar or borrowed via Occitan/French compas, from Vulgar Latin *compassāre ('to measure by paces'), built on com- + passus ('step, pace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: compás
Wiktionary — compás

con.etymology: The preposition con continues Latin cum ('with'), marking accompaniment, ingredients (café con leche, té con miel), tools, or manner (con cuidado).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: con

con.notes: With singular personal pronouns mí, ti and reflexive sí, Latin cum fused twice to produce the special forms conmigo, contigo and consigo.

concierto.etymology: Deverbal noun from concertar ('to arrange, harmonize, agree', with the musical sense reinforced by Italian concerto), from Late Latin concertāre ('to contend, act together').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: concierto
Wiktionary — concierto

conectar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cōnectere / connectere ('to bind or fasten together', from com- + nectere 'to tie'), reinforced in modern technical usage by English to connect.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conectar
Wiktionary — conectar

conmigo.etymology: Conmigo continues Latin mēcum ('with me'), to which Vulgar Latin re-prefixed cum (*cum mēcum > conmigo) once the final -cum was no longer felt clearly as 'with'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conmigo

conmigo.notes: Always written as one word, replacing *con mí in Spanish alongside contigo ('with you') and consigo ('with oneself').

conocer.etymology: Conocer continues Latin cognoscĕre ('to become acquainted with, recognize, know').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conocer

conocer.notes: Used for familiarity with people and places (¿Conoce usted esta calle?), whereas saber covers facts and skills.

conseguir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *consequīre, a regularized active form of Classical Latin deponent consequī ('to follow closely, overtake, attain, obtain'), from com- + sequī ('to follow').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conseguir
Wiktionary — conseguir

contar.etymology: Inherited from Latin computāre ('to sum up, reckon, calculate; relate a story'), formed from com- + putāre ('to trim, reckon, consider'), with syncope and assimilation of -mp't- to -nt-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contar
Wiktionary — contar

contra.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin contrā ('against, opposite, facing, in return for').

Wiktionary — contra

contratar.etymology: Formed in Spanish from contrato ('contract, formal agreement', < Latin contractus) + -ar ('to engage by contract, hire').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contratar
Wiktionary — contratar

contrato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin contractus ('a drawing together, bargain, legal agreement'), derived from contrahere (com- + trahere 'to draw together').

history.meaning: to draw together, conclude a deal

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contrato
Wiktionary — contrato

contraventana.etymology: Compound formed in Spanish from contra- ('against, protective outer layer') + ventana ('window', originally 'wind-opening', from Latin ventus 'wind').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: contraventana
Wiktionary — contraventana

conversión.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin conversiō, conversiōnis ('a turning around, transformation, change'), derived from convertere ('to turn around, transform').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: conversión
Wiktionary — conversión

convertir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *convertīre, reshaped from Classical Latin convertere ('to turn around, transform, alter'), from com- + vertere ('to turn').

history.meaning: to turn / to turn around, transform

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: convertir
Wiktionary — convertir

corazón.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corāciōne (or *corāceum + -ōne), an affective/augmentative formation built on Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corazón
Wiktionary — corazón

corbata.etymology: Borrowed via Italian corvatta / cravatta (and French cravate) from Serbo-Croatian Hrvat ('Croat'), after the linen neckscarves worn by 17th-century Croatian light cavalrymen.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corbata
Wiktionary — corbata

correcto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin correctus ('straightened, amended, accurate'), past participle of corrigere (com- + regere 'to guide, make straight').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: correcto
Wiktionary — correcto

correr.etymology: Inherited from Latin currere ('to run, hasten, flow'), showing regular lowering of short u to o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: correr
Wiktionary — correr

cortar.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtāre ('to shorten, clip, cut off'), derived from the adjective curtus ('short, clipped').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cortar
Wiktionary — cortar

corteza.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corticea ('bark, rind, crust'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin corticeus ('of bark'), derived from cortex, corticis ('tree bark, outer shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corteza
Wiktionary — corteza

corto.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtus ('clipped, shortened, brief, short'), with regular lowering of short u to o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: corto
Wiktionary — corto

costar.etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnstāre ('to stand firm, stand at a price, cost'), formed from com- + stāre ('to stand'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -nst- to -st-.

history.meaning: to stand at a price, cost

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: costar
Wiktionary — costar

crecer.etymology: Crecer continues Latin crescĕre. The Spanish verb covers physical growth in people and plants as well as increases in size, intensity or activity.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crecer

crecer.notes: In the first person singular present (crezco), -c- alternates with -zc- before -o, just like conocer (conozco) and parecer (parezco).

creer.etymology: Inherited from Latin crēdere ('to trust, entrust, believe'), with regular loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: creer
Wiktionary — creer

crema.etymology: Entered Spanish from French crème (Old French cresme), which blended Late Latin chrisma ('anointing unguent', from Greek khrîsma) with Gaulish crama ('milk cream').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crema

crema.notes: Covers dairy cream, rich pastry curds (crema de limón), and puréed vegetable soups.

cremallera.etymology: Borrowed from French crémaillère ('toothed pot-hook, rack gear, zipper'), from Old French cremail, descending via Late Latin *cremasculus from Ancient Greek κρεμαστήρ (kremastḗr, 'hanger, suspender').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cremallera
Wiktionary — cremallera

cristal.etymology: Descends from Latin crystallus, borrowed from Greek krýstallos ('clear ice, rock crystal'), derived from krýos ('icy cold, frost').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cristal

cristal.notes: In everyday Peninsular Spanish, el cristal is also the standard word for a windowpane or spectacle lens.

crujiente.etymology: Active participial adjective derived from crujir ('to crunch, crackle, creak') + -nte, an expressive verb of onomatopoeic origin.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: crujiente
Wiktionary — crujiente

cruzar.etymology: Cruzar is formed within Romance from cruz ('cross', from Latin crux, crucis), originally meaning to lay across or pass from one side to the other.

RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cruz

cruzar.notes: Spelling changes -z- to -c- before -e (crucé el puente).

cuaderno.etymology: Cuaderno continues Late Latin quaternus ('folded sheet of four leaves', from quattuor, 'four'), how medieval notebooks and quires were bound.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuaderno

cuaderno.notes: Modern Spanish standard word for a bound notebook or exercise book.

cuadro.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin quadrum ('square, four-sided figure'), neuter noun related to quattuor ('four'), later applied to a framed canvas or picture.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuadro

cuando.etymology: Inherited from Latin quandō ('when, at what time, since').

cuarenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quarranta, contracted from Classical Latin quadrāgintā ('forty'), a derivative of quattuor ('four').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuarenta

cuarto.etymology: Cuarto descends from Latin quartus ('fourth, quarter'), developing senses for a quarter-hour (y cuarto), a fourth floor or share, and a room.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuarto

cuarto.notes: In clock time, y cuarto means quarter past and menos cuarto means quarter to (never feminine *cuarta, because cuarto here is the masculine noun 'a quarter').

cuatro.etymology: Cuatro continues Latin quattuor ('four'), with regular metathesis of final -or > -ro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuatro

cuatro.notes: Used bare after la habitación (la habitación cuatro = Room 4) and with las for clock time (las cuatro).

cubo.etymology: Conflates two Latin words: 'bucket, pail, wheel hub' inherited from Vulgar Latin *cūpus (masculine variant of Classical Latin cūpa 'tub, vat'); and geometric 'cube' borrowed from Latin cubus (< Greek κύβος 'die, cube').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cubo
Wiktionary — cubo

cuchara.etymology: Cuchara descends from Latin cochleāre ('spoon with a pointed handle originally used for eating snails and eggs'), derived from cochlea ('snail shell'), borrowed from Greek kokhlías.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuchara

cuchara.notes: Cognate with Portuguese colher and French cuillère.

cucharada.etymology: Formed within Spanish from cuchara ('spoon', < Latin cochleāre) + the capacity suffix -ada ('spoonful').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cucharada
Wiktionary — cucharada

cucharilla.etymology: Diminutive formed in Spanish from cuchara ('spoon') + -illa ('teaspoon'); cuchara descends from Latin cochleāre ('spoon for eating snails'), from cochlea ('snail shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cucharilla
Wiktionary — cucharilla

cuenco.etymology: Masculine formation alongside cuenca ('deep clay or wooden bowl'), inherited from Latin concha ('shell, shell-shaped vessel'), from Ancient Greek κόγχη (kónkhē, 'mussel shell').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuenco
Wiktionary — cuenco

cuerda.etymology: Cuerda continues Latin chorda ('catgut, musical string, cord'), borrowed from Greek khordḗ ('gut string of a lyre').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuerda

cuerda.notes: Short stressed Latin ŏ diphthongized regularly to ue (chŏrda > cuerda).

cuero.etymology: Inherited from Latin corium ('thick hide, skin, leather'), with regular diphthongization of short o to ue before yod.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuero
Wiktionary — cuero

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidado
Wiktionary — cuidado

cuidar.etymology: Cuidar continues Latin cōgitāre ('to think, reflect, attend carefully to'), shifting in Old Spanish from 'ponder' to 'look after, take care of'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuidar

cuidar.notes: Can take a direct object or de (cuidar las plantas / cuidar de las plantas).

culpa.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin culpa ('fault, blame, moral or legal responsibility').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: culpa
Wiktionary — culpa

curiosear.etymology: Formed within Spanish from curioso ('curious, inquisitive', < Latin cūriōsus) + the frequentative verbal suffix -ear ('to browse, pry, look around curiously').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curiosear
Wiktionary — curiosear

curiosidad.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsitās, cūriōsitātis ('eagerness for knowledge, inquisitiveness'), derived from cūriōsus ('careful, inquisitive').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curiosidad

curioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsus ('bestowing care, diligent, inquisitive'), derived from cūra ('care, attention').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: curioso
Wiktionary — curioso

cuál.etymology: Interrogative pronoun and determiner ('which?, what one?'), inherited from Latin quālis ('of what kind, which'), written with an accent mark to distinguish it from relative cual.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuál
Wiktionary — cuál

cuándo.etymology: Interrogative adverb ('when?'), inherited from Latin quandō ('at what time?'), written with an acute accent in direct and indirect questions.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuándo
Wiktionary — cuándo

cuánto.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative determiner, pronoun, and adverb ('how much?, how many?'), inherited from Latin quantus ('how great, how much'), written with an accent mark to distinguish it from relative cuanto.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cuánto
Wiktionary — cuánto

cálido.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin calidus ('warm, hot', derived from calēre 'to be warm'), forming a learned doublet alongside inherited popular caldo ('broth').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cálido
Wiktionary — cálido

cómo.etymology: Interrogative and exclamative adverb ('how?'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *quōmo, a shortened form of Classical Latin quōmodo ('in what manner, how').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cómo
Wiktionary — cómo

cómodo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commodus ('having due measure, suitable, convenient, comfortable'), formed from com- + modus ('measure, manner').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: cómodo
Wiktionary — cómodo

dado.etymology: As a noun ('playing die, small cube'), traced by the DLE to Classical Arabic aʿdād ('numbers') or Late Latin datum ('that which is cast or given'); as a participle ('given'), inherited from Latin datus (past participle of dare).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dado
Wiktionary — dado

dar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin dare ('to give, offer, hand over, grant').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dar
Wiktionary — dar

de.etymology: The preposition de continues Latin dē ('from, down from, concerning'), absorbing most functions of the Latin genitive case across Romance languages.

de.notes: De expresses possession (la llave de Clara), material (de madera, de latón), origin, contents (una taza de té), and part of the day after clock hours (de la mañana).

debajo.etymology: Formed in Old Spanish by compounding the preposition de (< Latin dē) with bajo ('low, underneath', < Late Latin bassus).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: debajo
Wiktionary — debajo

deber.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre ('to owe, be bound to, ought'), itself a contraction of dē- + habēre ('to have from another, keep on loan').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: deber
Wiktionary — deber

decibelio.etymology: Twentieth-century scientific borrowing (via English decibel / French décibel), combining Latin decimus ('tenth', deci-) + belio, named in honor of telecommunications pioneer Alexander Graham Bell (1847–1922).

history.meaning: tenth of a bel (unit of sound intensity)

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decibelio
Wiktionary — decibelio

decidido.etymology: Participial adjective of decidir ('decided, resolute, determined'), borrowed from Latin dēcīdere ('to cut off, settle a matter, decide', from dē- + caedere 'to cut').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: decidido
Wiktionary — decidido

decir.notes: Querer decir means to mean, and the polite imperative dígame is standard in Spain when answering the telephone or welcoming a customer.

dedicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēdicāre ('to proclaim, consecrate, devote to a purpose'), formed from dē- + dicāre ('to proclaim, dedicate').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dedicar
Wiktionary — dedicar

dedo.etymology: Dedo descends from Latin digĭtus ('finger, toe') through regular loss of the unstressed internal vowel and voicing of -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dedo

dedo.notes: Covers both fingers (dedos de la mano) and toes (dedos del pie); learned cognate dígito means 'numerical digit'.

dejar.etymology: The DLE traces dejar to Vulgar Latin *daxāre, altered from Classical Latin laxāre ('to loosen, release, let go') under influence of dare/delinquĕre.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dejar

dejar.notes: Covers leaving an object behind, letting someone do something, or stopping an action (dejar de + infinitive).

del.etymology: Del is the obligatory contraction of preposition de ('of, from') + masculine singular definite article el ('the').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delante
Wiktionary — delante

delantero.etymology: Formed within Spanish from delante ('in front, ahead') + the relational suffix -ero ('situated in front, front, forward').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delantero
Wiktionary — delantero

delicioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēliciōsus ('delightful, delicious, luxurious'), derived from Classical Latin dēliciae ('delight, pleasure, charm').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: delicioso
Wiktionary — delicioso

demasiado.etymology: Originally the past participle of obsolete demasiar ('to exceed'), derived from demasía ('excess, surplus'), which was built on demás (de + más, < Latin dē + magis 'more').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: demasiado
Wiktionary — demasiado

dentro.etymology: Dentro continues Latin de intro ('from within, inside'), fusing preposition de with adverb intro.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: dentro

dentro.notes: Dentro de marks both spatial interior (dentro de la maleta) and time until a future event (dentro de cuarenta minutos = in forty minutes' time).

depender.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēpendēre ('to hang down from, be dependent upon'), formed from dē- + pendēre ('to hang').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: depender

guardar.notes: Everyday Spanish uses guardar for putting something away safely in a drawer, pocket or storeroom as well as keeping a secret.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lado

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: latón

latón.notes: Prized for piano pedals, shutter pins, and door hardware because it polishes brightly and resists rust.

leche.notes: Feminine noun in Spanish (la leche fría, café con leche), unlike masculine French lait and Italian latte.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: lenteja

lenteja.notes: Optical lenses (lentes) took their name from the biconvex shape of a lentil seed.

les.etymology: Les continues Latin dative plural illīs ('to them'), marking plural indirect objects ('to them' or formal plural 'to you all', ustedes).

letra.etymology: Letra develops from Latin littĕra ('written character; in the plural, epistle or learning').

letra.notes: Singular la letra also means 'a person's handwriting' (la letra de mi tía) and 'song lyrics'.

libro.etymology: Libro continues Latin liber, librī ('inner bark of a tree, scroll, book').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: libro

libro.notes: El libro de reservas is a hotel's reservation ledger.

limonero.etymology: Limonero adds the Spanish fruit-tree suffix -ero (from Latin -ārius) to limón ('lemon') to name the lemon tree.

limón.notes: Drops its written accent in the plural: los limones.

llave.notes: Feminine noun: la llave, las llaves; llave inglesa ('English key') means an adjustable spanner/wrench.

lluvia.etymology: Lluvia continues Latin pluvia ('rain'), with initial Latin pl- palatalizing regularly to Castilian ll-.

los.notes: Los dos means 'both of them'; los lunes means 'on Mondays'.

luego.etymology: Luego descends from Latin locō (ablative of locus, 'on the spot, immediately'), which shifted in Spanish from 'right away' to 'then, afterwards, later'.

manzanilla.notes: Mirrors the exact semantic motivation of Greek khamaímēlon ('ground-apple', > English chamomile).

martes.etymology: Continues Latin [diēs] Martis ('day of Mars'), preserving the Latin genitive ending -is as invariable -es.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: martes

martes.notes: Like lunes, miércoles, jueves, and viernes, its singular and plural forms are identical (el martes / los martes).

mañana.etymology: Mañana derives from Vulgar Latin *(hora) maneāna ('early morning hour', from Latin māne, 'in the morning').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mañana

mañana.notes: Feminine la mañana means 'the morning' (por la mañana, ¡Hasta mañana!), whereas adverbial mañana with no article means 'tomorrow'.

me.etymology: The unstressed pronoun me continues Latin accusative me (with dative mihi merging in Vulgar Latin), marking the speaker as direct object, indirect object, or reflexive participant.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

me.notes: Unstressed me stands before finite verbs (me encanta, me llamo) and attaches to the end of infinitives, gerunds and affirmative imperatives (dígame, déjame).

medio.etymology: Medio continues Latin medius ('middle, half'), inflecting as an adjective for 'half' (media hora, a las siete y media).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: medio

medio.notes: In clock time y media is feminine because it agrees with implied media hora ('half an hour').

mediodía.etymology: Mediodía fuses medio ('middle') + día ('day') on the pattern of Latin merīdiēs ('midday, noon').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mediodía

mediodía.notes: Masculine singular compound noun: al mediodía means 'at noon'.

melodía.etymology: The DLE traces melodía through Late Latin melodĭa to Greek melōidía ('choral song, tune'), from mélos ('song, musical phrase') and ōidḗ ('singing').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: melodía

melodía.notes: Carries a written accent on í to show that -ía forms two syllables.

mercado.etymology: Mercado continues Latin mercātus ('trade, buying and selling, marketplace'), derived from mercāri ('to trade').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mercado

mercado.notes: Refers both to a covered municipal market hall and to open-air neighbourhood stalls.

mesa.etymology: Mesa continues Latin mēnsa ('table'), with early spoken Latin loss of -n- before -s- (*mēsa).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mesa

mesa.notes: Poner la mesa means 'to set the table'.

mi.etymology: Unstressed possessive determiner mi ('my') developed as the proclitic shortening of Old Spanish mío/mía (from Latin meus, mea) before a singular noun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mi

mi.notes: Same form before masculine and feminine nouns (mi hermano, mi maleta); plural adds -s (mis llaves). No accent, unlike prepositional mí.

miel.etymology: Miel descends from Latin mel, mellis ('honey'), with regular Castilian diphthongization of short stressed ĕ to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: miel

miel.notes: Feminine noun in modern standard Spanish: la miel dorada, miel de flores.

mirar.etymology: Mirar continues Latin mīrārī ('to wonder at, gaze in admiration'), weakening in Romance to the ordinary active verb 'to look at, watch'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mirar

mirar.notes: Imperatives mira (tú), mire (usted) and mirad (vosotros) are constantly used in conversation to draw attention ('look!').

mismo.etymology: The DLE reconstructs Vulgar Latin *metipsĭmus behind mismo. It combines the emphatic element -met with a superlative of Latin ipse, meaning the same. The asterisk marks the reconstructed form.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mismo

history.meaning: an intensified form related to the same

mismo.notes: Mismo still expresses identity or emphasis. In ahora mismo it reinforces the time expression rather than agreeing with a person.

miércoles.etymology: Descends from Latin [diēs] Mercŭriī (reshaped in Vulgar Latin as *Mercŏris, 'day of Mercury'), with short stressed ĕ diphthongizing to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: miércoles

miércoles.notes: Retains proparoxytonic stress and invariable plural los miércoles.

modelo.etymology: Modelo was borrowed from Italian modello. The DLE takes that word back through reconstructed Vulgar Latin *modellus to Latin modŭlus, associated with measure or a measured rhythm. The asterisk identifies the reconstructed stage.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: modelo

history.meaning: a diminutive formation behind Italian modello

modelo.notes: Spanish uses modelo both for a pattern to copy and for a person who models. A person can be el modelo or la modelo.

moneda.etymology: Moneda continues Latin monēta, originally an epithet of Juno Moneta near whose Roman temple coins were minted.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: moneda

moneda.notes: Means an individual metal coin (unas monedas) as well as currency in general.

montaña.etymology: The DLE traces montaña to Vulgar Latin *montanĕa, from Latin montānus ('mountainous'), built on mons, montis ('mountain').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: montaña

montaña.notes: Used figuratively in una montaña de ('a huge pile of').

mostrador.etymology: Mostrador derives from mostrar ('to show, display', from Latin monstrāre) + instrument/place suffix -dor: originally a shop counter where goods were laid out to show customers.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrador
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mostrar

mostrador.notes: Standard Spanish word for a hotel reception desk, café bar counter, or shop counter.

muchísimo.etymology: Muchísimo combines mucho (from Latin multus) with the learned superlative suffix -ísimo (from Latin -issĭmus) to express 'very much' or 'a great deal'.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: -ísimo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas: mucho

muchísimo.notes: Muchísimo inflects as an adjective before nouns (muchísimas gracias) and stays invariable as an adverb after verbs.

morphemes.meaning: large amount or degree, from mucho

mudo.etymology: Mudo continues Latin mūtus ('mute, silent, unable to speak'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mudo

mudo.notes: Applied to silent letters (la hache muda) and to a piano key whose hammer fails to strike.

mueble.etymology: Continues Latin mōbilis ('movable', from movēre 'to move'): originally bienes muebles ('movable goods', as opposed to real estate), narrowed to household furniture.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mueble

mundo.etymology: Mundo continues Latin mundus. The DLE describes the world sense of that Latin word as a semantic calque of Greek kósmos: the meaning was modelled on the Greek expression rather than its sound being borrowed.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mundo

mundo.notes: Todo el mundo uses world collectively for everyone and takes a singular verb.

muro.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin mūrus ('stone wall, city wall').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muro

muro.notes: Typically denotes a thick exterior or load-bearing stone wall, whereas la pared (< pariēs) is an interior wall.

muy.etymology: Muy is a shortened form of older muito, which continues Latin multum. The DLE also identifies it as a reduced form of mucho; this older family therefore supplies both very and much in modern Spanish.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: muy
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mucho

muy.notes: In muy claro it raises the degree of clear. It does not change for the number or gender of the people involved.

más.etymology: Más developed through the older form maes from Latin magis. The modern word expresses a greater quantity or degree and can also intensify a comparison.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: más

más.notes: Más de before a number sets a threshold: más de veinticinco means more than twenty-five.

mí.etymology: Mí continues Latin dative pronoun mihi ('to me'). In modern Spanish it survives as the stressed first-person singular pronoun used after prepositions (para mí, cerca de mí).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: mí
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: yo
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: me

mí.notes: The written accent distinguishes prepositional pronoun mí ('me') from unaccented possessive determiner mi ('my').

nadie.etymology: Nadie evolved from Old Spanish nadi, continuing the Latin plural phrase (homĭnēs) nātī ('people born', i.e. 'any living soul') used in negative clauses.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nadie

nadie.notes: Stands alone before the verb (Nadie dice que no) or pairs with no before the verb (No hay nadie).

negro.etymology: Negro continues Latin niger, nigra, nigrum ('glossy black, dark'), with short Latin ĭ lowering regularly to Castilian e.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: negro

negro.notes: Té negro is black tea; for black espresso coffee in Spain, speakers normally say un café solo.

nevera.etymology: Nevera derives from nieve ('snow', from Latin nix, nivis) + place suffix -era: historically an icehouse packed with mountain snow to preserve food, now the household refrigerator.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nevera
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieve

nevera.notes: La nevera (alongside el frigorífico) is the everyday Peninsula Spanish word for fridge.

nieve.etymology: Continues Latin nix, nivis (accusative nivem, 'snow'), reshaped with diphthong ie by analogy with the verb nieva (< Vulgar Latin *nĕvat).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nieve

nieve.notes: Blanco como la nieve is a proverbial comparison for spotless white fabric.

no.etymology: No continues Latin nōn ('not'). In Spanish it serves both as the standalone negative answer ('no') and as the preverbal negator placed directly before the verb phrase.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: no

no.notes: When negative words like nadie or nada follow the verb, no still precedes the verb (No hay nadie en el patio).

noche.etymology: Noche descends regularly from Latin nox, noctis ('night'), showing palatalization of medial -ct- > -ch- (compare leche < *lacte, ocho < octo).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: noche

noche.notes: Esta noche means 'tonight', anoche means 'last night', and ¡Buenas noches! serves as both 'good evening' after dark and 'good night'.

nogal.etymology: Derived with the tree-collective suffix -al from Vulgar Latin *nucālis, built on Latin nux, nucis ('walnut, nut').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nogal

nos.etymology: Unstressed object and reflexive pronoun nos ('us, to us, ourselves') continues Latin accusative/dative nōs unchanged.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nos

nos.notes: Also marks reciprocal action: ¡Nos vemos! ('See you!', literally 'we see each other') and nos tuteamos ('we use tú with each other').

nosotros.etymology: Nosotros fused Old Spanish nos ('we', from Latin nōs) with otros ('others', from Latin altĕrōs), originally contrasting 'we ourselves (as opposed to others)' before becoming the standard subject pronoun.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nosotros

nosotros.notes: Feminine nosotras is used when an all-female group speaks of itself.

nuestro.etymology: Nuestro continues Vulgar Latin *noster, nostra, nostrum ('our, ours'), showing diphthongization of short stressed ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuestro

nuestro.notes: Agrees in gender and number with the thing possessed (nuestro barrio, nuestra puerta, nuestros clientes).

nueve.etymology: Nueve descends from Latin novem ('nine'), with stressed short ŏ diphthongizing regularly to Castilian ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nueve

nuevo.etymology: Nuevo continues Latin novus ('new, fresh, recent'), diphthongizing stressed short ŏ to ue.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: nuevo

nuevo.notes: De nuevo means 'again' (¡Buenos días de nuevo! = Good morning again!).

o.etymology: The conjunction o ('or') continues Latin aut ('or'), with Latin au monophthongizing regularly to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: o

o.notes: Changes spelling and sound to u before words starting with /o/ (o- or ho-, e.g. siete u ocho).

ocho.etymology: Ocho descends regularly from Latin octō ('eight'), with medial -ct- palatalizing to Castilian -ch-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ocho

ocho.notes: Las ocho en punto means 'eight o'clock sharp'.

octava.etymology: Learned feminine form of Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octo 'eight'), short for octāva consonántia ('eighth note of the diatonic scale').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: octava

octava.notes: The popular inherited outcome of octāvus is ochavo (a historic copper coin).

oficio.etymology: Oficio continues Latin officium, duty, service or function. Spanish uses it for a skilled trade or craft learned through practice as well as an official duty or occupation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oficio

oficio.notes: Compare el oficio (a skilled craft or trade) with la oficina (an office room or workplace).

oliva.etymology: Oliva continues Latin olīva ('olive fruit, olive tree'), an ancient Mediterranean borrowing cognate with archaic Greek *elaiwa (Classical Greek elaía).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oliva

oliva.notes: In standard Spanish aceite de oliva is universal, while the table fruit is called oliva in eastern Spain and aceituna elsewhere.

once.etymology: Once continues Latin undĕcim ('eleven', literally one + ten) via Vulgar Latin *undĕce > Old Spanish onze > once.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: once

once.notes: Las once y veinte means 'eleven twenty'.

ordenador.etymology: Ordenador ('computer' in Spain) was adapted from French ordinateur (coined in 1955 from Latin ordinātor, 'one who puts things in order', from ordināre).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: ordenador

ordenador.notes: Standard word for computer across Spain (while computadora or computador is used in Latin America).

oreja.etymology: Inherited from Latin auricŭla ('earlobe, outer ear'), diminutive of auris ('ear'), with regular monophthongization au > o and palatalization -c'l- > -j-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oreja

oreja.notes: Spanish distinguishes la oreja (outer ear) from el oído (< audītus, inner ear and musical hearing).

otoño.etymology: Otoño continues Latin autumnus ('autumn') through regular Romance monophthongization of au- to o- and palatalization of -mn- to -ñ-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: otoño

otoño.notes: Used without an article after en when speaking of the season in general (en otoño).

oír.etymology: Oír continues Latin audīre ('to hear'), with au > o and loss of intervocalic -d- leaving a two-syllable hiatus marked by the accent on -ír.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: oír

oír.notes: Irregular present stem oigo, oyes, oye, oímos, oís, oyen; ¡Oye! / ¡Oiga! is a common way to get someone's attention.

pan.etymology: Pan continues Latin pānis ('bread, loaf'), dropping final unstressed -e after -n in singular Castilian.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pan

para.etymology: Para developed from Old Spanish pora, fusing Latin pro ('for, on behalf of') + ad ('to, toward') to express destination, recipient, deadline and purpose.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: para

para.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive, para expresses 'in order to' (para abrir la puerta).

pasar.etymology: Pasar derives from Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to take steps, pass through'), built on Classical Latin passus ('step, pace').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pasar

pasar.notes: Covers walking past a landmark, handing something over (pásame la llave), spending time, happening (¿Qué pasa?), and welcoming someone inside (¡Pase usted!).

paseo.etymology: Paseo is a noun derived from the verb pasear ('to stroll'), ultimately from paso ('step, pace').

pasillo.etymology: Diminutive of paso ('step, passage', from Latin passus) formed with -illo: originally a narrow passage or short step, generalized to an indoor hallway or corridor.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pasillo

patio.etymology: The DLE marks patio ('inner courtyard') as of uncertain origin, likely through Occitan or Catalan pati from a Vulgar Latin derivative of patēre ('to lie open to the sky').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: patio

patio.notes: Heart of traditional Spanish town buildings, bringing daylight, lemon trees and fresh air to surrounding galleries.

paño.etymology: Inherited from Latin pannus ('piece of woven cloth, rag'), with geminate -nn- palatalizing regularly to -ñ-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: paño

paño.notes: Everyday word for a soft wiping, polishing, or kitchen cloth.

pedir.etymology: Pedir continues Latin petĕre ('to head for, seek, request'), shifting to the -ir conjugation with regular voicing of -t- > -d-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pedir

pedir.notes: Stem vowel alternates e -> i (pido, pide, pidió); pedir means to request or order (whereas preguntar means to ask a question).

pequeño.etymology: The DLE traces pequeño ('small, little, young') to an expressive Ibero-Romance *pikk- / *pett- root for tiny things (compare Italian piccolo and French petit).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pequeño

pequeño.notes: Used as an adjective (una calle pequeña) or noun for a young child (el pequeño = the younger boy).

perdonar.etymology: Perdonar continues Medieval Latin perdonāre ('to grant wholeheartedly, remit a debt, forgive', from per- + donāre, 'to give').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdonar

perdonar.notes: Imperative perdona (tú) or perdone (usted) is a polite everyday way to get someone's attention ('excuse me').

perdón.etymology: Perdón is the deverbal noun of perdonar (from Medieval Latin perdonāre), used standalone as an immediate apology ('sorry! / pardon me!').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdón
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: perdonar

perdón.notes: Perdón por el retraso / perdón por el error means 'sorry for the delay / mistake'.

pero.etymology: The conjunction pero comes from Latin per hoc, meaning because of or through this. Its modern contrastive use introduces a qualification or a different point after the first part of a statement.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pero

pero.notes: The conjunction is a different dictionary entry from the unrelated fruit name pero.

pie.etymology: Descends from Latin pēs, pedis (accusative pedem, 'foot'), losing intervocalic -d- and diphthongizing short stressed ĕ > ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pie

pie.notes: Forms core idioms such as estar de pie ('to stand') and ir a pie ('to go on foot').

piedra.etymology: Piedra continues Latin petra ('rock, stone', borrowed from Ancient Greek pétra), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie and -tr- voicing to -dr-.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: piedra

piedra.notes: De piedra ('made of stone', e.g. el puente de piedra) links material with de.

piel.etymology: Piel descends directly from Latin pellis ('skin, hide, pelt'), with stressed short ĕ diphthongizing to ie.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: piel

piel.notes: Covers human skin, thin fruit peel (la piel del limón), and dressed leather.

planta.etymology: Planta continues Latin planta ('sprout, shoot; sole of the foot'), extending from a living plant and ground footprint to each storey or floor of a building.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: planta

planta.notes: In Spain la planta baja is the ground floor, la primera planta is one flight up, and la segunda planta is two flights up.

plaza.etymology: Plaza descends from Vulgar Latin *plattea (Classical Latin platēa, 'broad street, courtyard', from Greek plateîa, 'wide way').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: plaza

plaza.notes: Diminutive la placita names a small, intimate neighbourhood square.

poco.etymology: Poco descends regularly from Latin paucus ('few, little'), with Latin au monophthongizing to Castilian o.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poco

poco.notes: Un poco de ('a little bit of') stays masculine singular even before feminine uncountable nouns (un poco de leche, un poco de agua).

poder.etymology: Poder evolved from Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularizing Classical Latin posse ('to be able, have power').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poder

poder.notes: Followed directly by an infinitive without any preposition (¿Puede ayudarme?, no puedo abrirla).

poner.etymology: Poner continues Latin pōnĕre ('to place, put, set down'), shifting to the Spanish second conjugation.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: poner

poner.notes: Irregular forms include pongo (1sg present), pon (tú command), puse/puso (preterite), and puesto (past participle).

por.etymology: Por merges Latin pro ('on behalf of, in exchange for, because of') and per ('through, along, by means of') into a single versatile Spanish preposition.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: por

por.notes: Marks parts of the day (por la mañana, por la tarde), movement through space (por el puente, por la escalera), and cause or motive (por favor).

porcelana.etymology: The DLE identifies porcelana as a borrowing from Italian porcellana, originally the glossy white cowrie shell and later applied to translucent Chinese ceramic ware whose glaze recalled the shell.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: porcelana

porcelana.notes: Besides teacups, classic electrical fuse carriers were traditionally made of white insulating porcelana.

posada.etymology: Posada derives from posar ('to lodge, rest, set down one's load', from Late Latin pausāre, 'to pause, halt for rest').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posada
RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: posar

posada.notes: Historically a traditional Spanish coaching inn where travellers paused for lodging and meals.

primavera.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra ('first spring'), reshaped from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the beginning of spring'), combining prīmus ('first') and vēr ('spring').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: primavera

progreso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōgressus ('a going forward, advance, progress'), action noun from prōgredī (prō- 'forward' + gradī 'to step, walk').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: progreso
Wiktionary — progreso

prometer.etymology: Inherited from Latin prōmittere ('to send forth, let go; to foretell, promise'), compounded from prō- ('forth, forward') and mittere ('to send').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: prometer
Wiktionary — prometer

pronto.etymology: Pronto continues Latin promptus. The Spanish word can refer to readiness or speed and also functions as an adverb for an early or near-future time.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: pronto

pronto.notes: Hasta pronto means see you soon; pronto does not describe the person’s character in this farewell.

propiedad.etymology: Inherited from Latin proprietātem (nominative proprietās, 'peculiarity, ownership, property'), derived from proprius ('one's own').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propiedad
Wiktionary — propiedad

propietario.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin proprietārius ('owner of property'), derived from Classical Latin proprietās ('ownership').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propietario
Wiktionary — propietario

propio.etymology: Semi-learned reflex of Latin proprius ('one's own, special, particular'), with dissimilatory loss of the second r (Old Spanish proprio > propio).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: propio
Wiktionary — propio

proporción.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prōportiōnem (nominative prōportiō, 'comparative relation, symmetry'), univerbated from prō portiōne ('according to each part').

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: proporción
Wiktionary — proporción

protegido.etymology: Participial adjective of proteger ('to protect, shelter'), from Latin prōtegere (prō- 'in front' + tegere 'to cover, roof').

tarde.notes: In Spain la tarde stretches from lunch until nightfall (roughly 2 p.m. to 8 or 9 p.m.), greeted with ¡Buenas tardes!.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tarea

tarea.notes: Cognate with Portuguese tarefa and English tariff (via Italian tariffa).

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: tarjeta

tarjeta.notes: Covers a luggage tag (una tarjeta de cartón), business card, postcard, or payment card (con tarjeta).

tarro.etymology: Word of uncertain origin (likely pre-Roman Iberian or expressive Mediterranean), denoting a wide-mouthed cylindrical jar or pot of glass or earthenware.

te.etymology: Unstressed pronoun te ('you, to you, yourself' for informal singular tú) continues Latin accusative tē unchanged.

sources.title: RAE–ASALE, Diccionario de la lengua española: te

tomar.notes: Most natural Spanish verb for ordering or having a drink or snack: ¿Qué va a tomar?, tomo un té con miel.
